messages.author: cfdb326818e8caf0
messages.subject: Beginner!
parts:
Hi, 

I am a beginner in statistical analysis, I am a Ph.D. student who would like to start using SEM. 

Actually, I feel lost a little bit but I am open to any advice to start using statistical analysis especially SEM using R. 

It will be very nice of you to give me a tip on how to begin in this area. 

Kind regards, 

K.

messages.author: 0325c6a976085eab
messages.subject: Re: Beginner!
parts:
I think the best advice depends on what you already know. If you know regression and factor analysis, then I like Loehlin's book (Latent Variable Models). Lots of people (including me) like Kline's book (Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling). There's also a Lavaan specific book (Latent Variable Modeling Using R). 

Dan Bauer and Patrick Curran have  set of videos on Youtube about SEM: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC7kcXN1Xoj4PzMIKPHJ5m7Q/videos (There are probably others as well). 

If you know multilevel models, have a look at the paper by Curran called "Have multilevel models been structural equation models all along". 

If you come from a more mathematical background, there are probably better resources, but I don't know them. :)

Personally, I think that learning SEM on your own is hard - ideally, you should find a course to take, and you should make use of online resources (like this group) to ask questions and find answers.

Jeremy

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Beginner!
parts:
Khaled,
  In addition to the books that Jeremy mentioned, I would not overlook Ken Bollen's book.  It is much more accessible than one might expect from other books from the same publisher.  There have been many new developments but Bollen covers the basics more thoroughly than other books.  So, reading Kline's book followed by Bollen's book would offer a good foundation to get you started.

  I would also add that you should approach learning SEM the way that you approach learning to ride a bicycle.  You can sit and read about it at great length but you will gain more from the reading if you couple it with practice.  It is not exactly muscle memory, but there is a comparable level of comfort with doing SEM analyses that you can only gain by working with the software and trying thing out firsthand.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
